content.title: What time will Artemis II reach the moon? How to watch live
content.text: April 6, 2026, 10:17 a.m. ETAmericans can soon watch astronauts reach the moon for the first time in more than 50 years.The Artemis II space mission is scheduled to complete its lunar flyby on Monday, April 6. Several sites will livestream the event.So, how can you see the moon through the astronaut's eyes? Here's what to know:What is Artemis II?Artemis II is the second mission under NASA's multibillion-dollar moon program. The mission launched on Wednesday, April 1, to send three Americans and one Canadian on a 10-day journey around the far side of the moon and back.The astronauts won't land on the moon, but instead observe it from the Orion shuttle. The astronauts will take photographs and record notes regarding the moon's surface. The crew will see areas of the far side of the moon never before seen directly by humans.The mission serves as a vital test flight to lay the groundwork for humans to make it back to the surface in as little as two years.When is Artemis II reaching the moon?The Artemis II crew is expected to reach the moon around 2:45 p.m. ET, according to NASA. The crew will then observe the moon for the next seven hours, during which they will see the near and far sides of the moon.How to watch Artemis II lunar flybyLive coverage begins at 1 p.m. ET on Monday, April 6, and continues through 9:45 p.m., according to NASA.The livestream will be available on:NASA+.Amazon Prime Video.Apple TV.Hulu.HBO Max.Netflix.Roku.NASA's YouTube page also provides 24/7 coverage of the mission.Is Netflix streaming Artemis II?Yes. Netflix struck a deal with NASA last summer to bring NASA+ to Netflix. The deal allows Netflix to stream rocket launches, astronaut spacewalks, mission coverage and more.Artemis II lunar flyby scheduleAll times are in Eastern and may change based on real-time operations, according to NASA.1 p.m.: Coverage of lunar flyby begins. 1:30 p.m.: NASA hosts a conversation between the crew and the science officer in NASA’s Mission Control Center in Houston to go over the objectives and timeline for the flyby.1:56 p.m.: The crew will surpass the record for humans’ farthest distance from Earth, previously set by Apollo 13 in 1970. Artemis II will reach a maximum distance of 252,760 miles from Earth, surpassing the record by about 4,105 miles.2:10 p.m.: Crew remarks on breaking Apollo 13 distance record (audio only).2:15 p.m.: Crew configures Orion’s cabin for flyby operations.2:45 p.m.: The seven-hour lunar observation begins.Because room at Orion’s windows is limited, the crew will divide into pairs, with two crew members observing for 55 to 85 minutes, while the other pair exercises or works on other tasks.6:44 p.m.: Mission control expects to temporarily lose communication with the crew as Orion passes behind the moon.7:02 p.m. Orion will make its closest approach to the moon (4,070 miles).At this distance, the moon will appear to the astronauts about the size of a basketball held at arm’s length.They also may be the first humans to see some parts of the moon's far side with the unaided eye.7:07 p.m.: Orion will once again reach its maximum distance from Earth.7:25 p.m.: NASA’s Mission Control Center should re-acquire communication with the astronauts. Earth should come back into view for the astroanuts.8:35-9:32 p.m.: The sun will pass behind the moon from the crew’s perspective, creating a solar eclipse.9:20 p.m.: Lunar observation concludes.The crew will begin transferring some of the imagery to the ground.NASA’s science team will review the images and observations overnight and then discuss them with the crew the following day.Artemis II live tracker. Where is Artemis II now?NASA has an Artemis II tracker available on its website and mobile app that allows users to see where Orion is, how fast it's traveling and how far the spacecraft is from both the Earth and the moon.Where did Artemis II launch from?The Artemis II mission launched from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. What is the goal of the Artemis II mission?The goal of NASA's Artemis campaign is to send astronauts to the surface of the moon for the first time since the Apollo missions came to an end in 1972, Florida Today reports.NASA is planning to establish a permanent foothold on the lunar south pole, using a series of crewed and uncrewed missions in the years ahead to build a moon base. From there, the first humans could head toward Mars.The 10-day mission primarily serves as a test flight, with the four-person crew testing systems and hardware ahead of a future moon landing.Meet the Artemis II crewThe four astronauts selected for the Artemis II mission include the first woman (mission specialist Christina Koch,) Black man (pilot Victor Glover) and Canadian (mission specialist Jeremy Hansen) to venture near the moon.The mission is under the command of NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman.Click here to learn more about the astronauts inside Orion and their expected roles during the spaceflight.How far is the moon from Earth?The moon is usually about 238,855 miles from Earth, per the Nashville Tennessean.However, that distance isn’t always the same, according to NASA, since the moon's orbit isn't a perfect circle. At its furthest point, the moon is located about 252,088 miles from Earth, but at its closest, the moon is roughly 225,623 miles away.USA TODAY Network Reporters Haadiza Ogwude, Eric Lagatta and Mariyam Muhammad contributed to this report.
